# Conformance

A port is not "done" when it compiles and produces random-looking bytes. It is
done when it reproduces the shared corpora exactly. This page describes the three
corpora, how to validate a new port, and why the usual smoke tests do not count.

The fixtures live in [`conformance/`](../conformance/). Nothing there is an
implementation — they are the numbers your port has to reproduce, generated by a
separate program (`fpsapcore`) from the one you are writing.

## The three corpora

### `ring_indices.csv` — the index tables (840 rows)

The four index sequences `x, y, z, w` for `i` in `[0, 840)`, one row per `i`.
Check this **first** in any port, because it is the one that fails silently (see
the [uint32 underflow trap](06-porting-guide.md#trap-1-the-uint32-underflow-in-the-ring-indices)).

If you would rather not parse the file, build the four tables and compare SHA-256
over the 840 raw bytes of each:

| table | SHA-256 |
|---|---|
| `x` | `408941a6f3d6aef71c0c85e73d2ff3293ad04a5791466a1188d1b1d1e50d3b7a` |
| `y` | `4ed70521d7e11ac671d3033ecb148d6fdb828b30e89fa2d634e90c31e17de877` |
| `z` | `df5d95d147ce57d0784c369765781ae97c644550afe6665be288a24cdc34b4ae` |
| `w` | `9bab2dd29089584c30562cb3dcd1d48676e86a239524742da13bfb83d2ecc752` |

### `sap_hash.csv` — one 64-byte block through the SAP hash (40 rows)

`block(64 bytes hex), sapHash(16 bytes hex)`. This is the right place to *start*
a port, because the SAP hash is where almost all of the difficulty lives — the
840-step ring loop over a 210-byte buffer, then the ~110-line byte circuit whose
statement order is load-bearing. If these 40 pass, the hard part is done.

Two of the rows are all-zero and all-`0xff`; the rest are pseudorandom from a
fixed seed.

### `bridge_x9head.csv` — the whole bridge (30 rows)

`localSAP(128 hex), gp(128 hex), x9head(20 hex)`. `gp` is Phase 1's 128-byte
output buffer; the 20 bytes out are the only payload-dependent input Phase 2
consumes. Row 0 uses the frozen local SAP the Go golden vectors pin, so it
cross-checks against those; the rest use fresh random ones, as a real sender
generates per session. Passing this means your port is a complete Phase-1 bridge.

## Why smoke tests do not count

Two failure modes have bitten this project repeatedly. Both pass a naive test:

- **The sharpest example is not a unit test at all.** Shairport Sync answers
  `/fp-setup` with `200 OK` — and answers a response with a deliberately flipped
  byte with `200 OK` too. Read as a pass, it "validated" this implementation
  while proving nothing, because it has no FairPlay to check against. The three
  HomePods that genuinely validate it refuse a single flipped bit. Acceptance is
  only evidence when refusal was possible.
- **Sensitivity is not discrimination.** A test that only checks a hash is
  deterministic, or that it changes when the payload changes, passes just as
  happily on a *wrong* implementation. The naive index derivation fails 39 of the
  40 SAP-hash vectors — and passes exactly one: **row 0, the all-zero block.** A
  ring loop over an all-zero buffer stays all-zero whichever cells it reads, so a
  smoke test on zeros proves nothing. It is in the corpus deliberately, as a
  demonstration of this trap.
- **A validator that shares an implementation with the thing it validates proves
  nothing.** Do not generate your expected indices with the same expression you
  are testing. Compare against these files or the digests, both of which came from
  a separate program.

## A fourth corpus: hardware-attested vectors

`testdata/hardware_attested.csv` is different in kind from the three above.
Those say *"this is what Apple's compiled code computed"*, because that is all
an archived emulator capture can tell you. These rows say something stronger:

> **A real HomePod was given this response and accepted it** — in a session
> where it refused a single flipped bit.

Captured 2026-08-04 from an `AudioAccessory5,1` on firmware `23L471` with
`ap2probe attest`. Twelve exchanges, all accepted, none rejected.

Each row is `challenge_hex, local_sap_hex, response_hex, verdict`. The response
depends on the sender's per-session local SAP as well as the challenge, so the
SAP is recorded too and the whole exchange **replays offline with no device and
no network** — `TestHardwareAttestedVectors` in `fpbridge` does exactly that.

`TestAttestedCorpusRejectsWrongAnswers` is the other half, and it is the part
that makes the corpus evidence rather than decoration: it flips single bits in
the challenge and in the local SAP and requires the response to change. A corpus
that cannot fail a wrong implementation proves nothing — the same argument this
page makes about the all-zero SAP-hash row, and the same argument the receiver
itself made by refusing a flipped bit.

This corpus is only obtainable now that pairing works; see
[Pairing](12-pairing.md).

## Validating a new port

1. Build the four index tables and check them against `ring_indices.csv` or the
   four digests. Fix any mismatch before proceeding — nothing downstream can be
   right if these are wrong.
2. Run your SAP hash over every `block` in `sap_hash.csv`; require 40/40.
3. Run your bridge over every `(localSAP, gp)` in `bridge_x9head.csv`; require
   30/30.
4. **Test where your language is weakest.** Run the checks under the build that
   turns the deliberate unsigned wraps into failures:
   - **Rust:** debug build (overflow checks on).
   - **C#:** `<CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow>`.
   - **C:** clean under `-Wpedantic -Wconversion`, and under UBSan + ASan.
   A port that only ever runs in release or unchecked mode has not been tested
   where it is weakest.

## Mutation testing: prove the corpus rejects wrong ports

The corpus is only as good as its ability to *reject*. The Python port asserts
exactly this: it deliberately introduces three specific porting mistakes (the
naive `(i+55)` index, an identity `rotl` in place of `rotateOrZero`, and a missing
`& 0xff` mask) and asserts the corpus **fails** on each. If you extend a port,
copy that idea — a corpus that cannot fail a known-wrong implementation is not
protecting you.

## Ports that pass

Every language in [`ports/`](../ports/) passes 40/40 SAP-hash and 30/30 bridge
vectors. See [`ports/README.md`](../ports/README.md) for the per-language status,
and the [API reference](08-api-reference.md) for each port's entry point.
